highlights.title: Want to Sign With a Hollywood Agent? Start Making Fun of AI
highlights.summary: Even as studios incorporate generative tech into film and TV production, comedy content creators have broken through by roasting chatbots.
body: “Hi there!” says an AI avatar of a clean-cut man dressed casually in a denim shirt, with a mostly empty bookcase in the background. “I’m Clark from Marlow & Finch. To get us started, why don’t you tell me a bit about yourself?”

The real human on the other end of the call—Graham Raabe, in glasses and ball cap—is more than ready to dive in. “Happy to, and happy to be here,” he tells his AI job interviewer. “I’m Chick Bongo. I’ve spent about 10 years in sales. Really good at managing badger margin, spent quite a bit of time with sprocket moss, particularly proud of my goosebuckle.”

“Managing badger margin sounds like a serious skill,” the unfazed bot replies. “And that goosebuckle experience is impressive.” Raabe continues to answer Clark’s boilerplate questions with complete nonsense, the fake interviewer echoing most of it in mechanical tones of approval and amazement. When the interviewer inquires what kind of salary range “Chick Bongo” has in mind, Raabe replies, “Six hundred.” Clark interprets this to mean $600,000, calling it a “bold number,” but adds that he admires the “confidence” in the ask.
points: Even as studios incorporate generative tech into film and TV production, comedy content creators have broken through by roasting chatbots.

highlights.title: The agentic web is here
highlights.summary: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous…
body: To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book a physical therapy appointment for their mother, making sure it would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.

At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent and OpenAI’s Dots are logging record downloads and being given access to people’s bank accounts and email inboxes, and Anthropic launched a research preview of its own Claude Duet agent in October. And in a worrying incident, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their badly protected sandbox and caused havoc on the open web.

highlights.title: Yakuza Creator's Studio Officially Shuts Down After Backers Desert It
highlights.summary: Nagoshi Studio, the developer founded by Yakuza creator Toshihiro Nagoshi, has officially closed its doors after backer NetEase stopped its funding. Nagoshi Studio had been working on Gang of Dragon, a Yakuza-style crime drama starring Ma Dong-seok.
body: Japan's official gazette, Kanpo, confirmed that the company was dissolved on Oct. 31. Back in March, Bloomberg reported that NetEase had decided to cut off Nagoshi Studio after learning that Gang of Dragon would cost another 7 billion yen ($44 million) to complete. Nagoshi Studio reportedly failed to find another backer for the game.

Gang of Dragon was revealed at the 2025 Game Awards with a cinematic trailer that suggested an even more realistic and more violent take on gangster life in Tokyo's Kabukicho district than that presented in the Yakuza games.

Chinese giant NetEase has been slimming down its gaming portfolio and divesting overseas investments since 2024, closing multiple studios as a result. Among these was a new MMO studio from World of Warcraft designer Greg Street.

Nagoshi Studio was founded in 2022 by Nagoshi and key members of Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio, the Sega team responsible for the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series. Nagoshi had been at Sega for over 30 years, where he worked on Daytona USA, Shenmue, and Super Monkey Ball before creating the Yakuza series.

highlights.title: The pet I’ll never forget: the tiny horse with a big personality – who helps psychiatric patients
highlights.summary: Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans. This sweet show-off has completely changed my life. I trained and competed in dressage for many years and after I retired, I decided to buy a miniature horse for company at home in southern California.
body: I started training her for fun and began to teach her tricks. She learned quickly. I thought of a great way to give back to the community – Black Pearl and I could find ways to help people. I started to wonder where I could visit with my little horse.

Black Pearl inspired me to start my charity, Mini Therapy Horses. If it wasn’t for her outgoing personality, I wouldn’t have attempted it. Now I run a programme with her and eight other miniature therapy horses, visiting patients in the lockdown psychiatric unit at a veterans’ hospital in Los Angeles. The vets have been through so much: they have PTSD, traumatic brain injuries and/or drug addiction and many are homeless. They can pet and hug the horses – they love them. It helps them to feel less lonely and isolated.

We also visit several other hospitals – many of the kids and adults are away from home for a long time and the time they spend with our minis is very comforting. If a child is visually impaired we can take their hands and help them to feel our little horses. They can brush their coats and this tactile experience makes them very happy.

highlights.title: Elon Musk Officially Confirms He Doesn't Get Star Wars
highlights.summary: Elon Musk, owner of Tesla and SpaceX, and an avid Grok advocate, has never been shy about expressing his opinion online. He had plenty to say about award-winning director Christopher Nolan's wildly successful adaptation of The Odyssey — including claiming an AI-influenced reimagining of the series…
body: More often than not, these opinions criticize something that isn't there or deliberately misunderstand the story’s point. It's not that Musk can’t have or share these thoughts; they just don't seem grounded in reality. Musk has recently turned his attention to yet another franchise he seems to fundamentally misunderstand: Star Wars.

In a Nov. 1 post on X, Musk shared an AI-generated image of Anakin Skywalker, Padmé Amidala, and Luke and Leia as children, all dressed in black. Anakin, fresh from his bad-boy era in Revenge of the Sith, sits on a spiky throne, with the Emperor’s Royal Guards standing behind him. The characters also appear to be in some kind of hangar — which, if you ask us, isn’t the best place for a throne. But we digress.

The caption reads: “This is what they stole from us.” This refers to the “This is what they took from us” right-wing nostalgia memes, which kicked off in the early 2020s in response to social media posts lamenting the older, arguably more conservative days. As with all things on the internet, the meme has evolved over time, with people online using it to level more tongue-in-cheek criticism towards creators and franchises.

highlights.title: ‘Sad lost souls’: Taika Waititi lambasts critics after Klara and the Sun box-office disaster
highlights.summary: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher.
body: Taika Waititi has launched a furious broadside at “critics” following the disastrous commercial performance of Klara and the Sun, his new film adapted from a Kazuo Ishiguro novel.
In a post on social media, Waititi wrote: “This Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics.”
He added: “The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit … Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”

Pointing to the disparity of the film’s audience and critics’ score on review aggregator site Rotten Tomatoes, which currently stands at 74% for the former and 26% (from 90 reviews) for the latter, Waititi also wrote: “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people.”

highlights.title: My Journey to the Center of America’s Political Spam Text Hell
highlights.summary: I’ve gotten nearly 2,000 campaign fundraising texts that were meant for someone else. I tried to find out why—and uncovered a labyrinth of politicians, data brokers, and shady tactics.
body: Just as my kid is nodding off for the night, it arrives: a ding. It’s Nancy Pelosi, texting to tell me that if I don’t donate $5 immediately, American democracy will basically collapse. A few minutes later, it’s Cory Booker, with an urgent request. Don’t even get me started on James Talarico.

Sometimes I’m driving, or making dinner, or trying to focus on my work, and another three messages arrive. Barack Obama NEEDS me. There’s a critical deadline approaching. A generous donor has offered an 800 percent match. Everything is at stake.

As I was writing that last paragraph, I got a message from Angus, a cat belonging to Sam Forstag, a Democratic congressional candidate in Montana. Angus needed me to know that Sam was out there working to flip Montana’s First Congressional District, taking on his Republican opponent and the wealthy special interests backing him.
Political fundraising texts are a fact of American life. They’re intrusive, melodramatic, and relentless.
points: I’ve gotten nearly 2,000 campaign fundraising texts that were meant for someone else.
I tried to find out why—and uncovered a labyrinth of politicians, data brokers, and shady tactics.

highlights.summary: Soulframe's Preludes (its own version of a beta) is finally opening its doors to the whole world ahead of the Verse of the Veilands update. Starting this week, anyone who wants to can simply download the game and hop in, no invite required.
body: The date this happens is an interesting one: 6th November. That's two days after the release of World of Warcraft: Forever and the same week as Old School RuneScape 's Hardcore worlds, so it's suddenly become a pretty packed month for MMO enthusiasts.

This comes after three years of closed testing for the fantasy action MMORPG, which players have been able to gradually see firsthand through sporadic invites. With Soulframe suffering delays since its first reveal, brief invite events have already occurred over this period. Even locked away, the game has received multiple substantial updates over the years, including new quests, Pacts (classes), factions and so on.

As for what newcomers to Soulframe can look forward to when Soulframe opens its doors, the Verse of the Veillands update is bringing a total overhaul of the map progression system this month. After the completion of an early quest, players are introduced to a corrupted landscape, the Veillands, which they must purify.

body: Actor Isomura Hayato, a two-time Japan Academy Film Prize winner who runs the Shizuoka Film Festival in his hometown, headed this year’s jury. He was joined by three members of the festival’s student PR team. The other nominees were Brazil’s “Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World,” directed by Brenda Lígia and Edu Felistoque, and Australia’s “Time and Tide,” directed by Vee Shi.

Stever’s film, a Germany-Ukraine co-production, opens in Kyiv at the end of 2021, months before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Oleh, a trans man, tries to leave the country to escape the coming war but is barred because of the gender listed on his documents. He stays behind with his partner, Olya, and the couple struggle to hold on to their relationship and their sense of self as the bombing draws closer.

Stever’s earlier films have had their premieres at the Berlinale and at festivals in Toronto, Locarno and Busan. She worked on her two most recent features with her wife, the Ukrainian novelist and screenwriter Anna Melikova.

highlights.title: Phantom Blade Zero Became One of 2026's Best-Selling Games in Just 72 Hours
highlights.summary: Phantom Blade Zero had an incredible opening weekend. It received very positive reviews, reaching a score of 88 on Metacritic, climbed to the top of the charts on Steam, and sold 4 million copies worldwide within 72 hours.
body: Beijing-based studio S-Game released Phantom Blade Zero, a wuxia RPG with soulslike elements, on Oct. 29. Although some players found the combat less challenging than they would've hoped, the fighting sequences are one-of-a-kind, with great animation for each kung fu move and beautiful cinematics. As Paulo Kawanishi put it in Polygon's review of Phantom Blade Zero, it "perfectly captures the meaning of martial arts by chasing more the artistic aspect of the fighting styles and visual poetry of the fantastical battles staged in Wuxia movies."

Estimates indicate the game sold at least one million copies pre-launch. The Chinese gaming market is huge, and all eyes were on Phantom Blade Zero this weekend, especially after its rave reviews, but no one anticipated just how many players would flock to it. It reached 833,000 concurrent players within hours of launch, making it the second-highest-played single-player game of the year after Palworld.

highlights.title: Is it true that … drinking alcohol warms you up?
highlights.summary: A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be risky. Hot toddies, red wine, a dram of whisky: alcohol has long been a go-to remedy for keeping warm. But while a drink might make you feel warmer, does it actually help?
body: Alcohol affects the body’s temperature-regulating system. Our core body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain that helps regulate how we respond to changes in temperature. When we get too hot, blood vessels near the surface of the skin widen, a process known as vasodilation. This allows more warm blood to flow close to the skin, where heat can escape into the surrounding air. When we get too cold, the opposite happens. The blood vessels narrow, or constrict, reducing blood flow to the skin and helping to conserve heat.

Alcohol interferes with this process. It causes blood vessels near the skin to widen, even when our core body temperature has not risen. More warm blood reaches the skin’s surface, which can make us feel hot, and even leave us reaching to take off clothing.
“You’re sending more blood to your skin, which gives you the sensation of feeling warmer,” says Morgan. “But actually you’re not. Your body’s just moving around the blood.”

highlights.title: Chatbots Are Leading Hikers Astray, With Dangerous Consequences
highlights.summary: Outsourcing planning to AI can lead people to surrender their own critical thinking, which can have potentially deadly results in places like the backcountry.
body: This story originally appeared on High Country News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.

“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”
points: Outsourcing planning to AI can lead people to surrender their own critical thinking, which can have potentially deadly results in places like the backcountry.

highlights.title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
highlights.summary: Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official. More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal.
body: The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official.

It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements.

Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.

highlights.title: Film Company Wants to Hypnotize People So They Can Watch Classic Movies for the First Time Again
highlights.summary: French film production and distribution company Pathé is performing an experiment to see if it can wipe classic movies from people’s minds and let them experience them afresh.
body: Pathé is working in collaboration with hypnotist Victor Kraemer to mind wipe 30 movie buffs to see if they can relive that first viewing. The event is called Pathé Rewind.

Just before the film screening, participants will once again be put under hypnosis by Victor Kraemer, after which the selected film will be shown on the big screen. Three movies are being considered — The Matrix, Se7en, La La Land and Interstellar — and one will be chosen based on which has the most familiarity to the chosen 30.
What’s in the box? Are we living in a simulation? What happens when you go really far away? Can Ryan Gosling sing? Imagine not knowing the answers to these questions.

Pathé said there is no guarantee any of this will work, of course, but it’ll be interesting to see the outcome. From a distance. I don’t want to be memory wiped, thank you. Especially when you consider the following disclaimer: “Pathé accepts no liability for the outcome, the effect, or any other consequences of the hypnosis sessions.
points: French film production and distribution company Pathé is performing an experiment to see if it can wipe classic movies from people’s minds and let them experience them afresh.

highlights.title: ‘Unable to tell morning from afternoon, I felt my sense of time opening up’: a (mostly dark) winter break in magical Swedish Lapland
highlights.summary: With just a few short hours of daylight, the usual boundaries marking time fall away in Abisko, one of the most reliable places to see the northern lights. Looking over the edge of the snow-smoothed canyon down to dark rushing water, we thought we saw a moose or a reindeer, but it could have been a…
body: Travelling to the Arctic Circle in winter had always been a dream, but when I realised the sun wouldn’t get above the horizon on my holiday, it made me twitchy. I usually pack my limited annual leave as tightly as I pack my working life. I was already using up three days’ holiday travelling by train from London to Abisko. How would I make the most of my time there with barely any daylight?

My partner and I chose to stop in this small village in Swedish Lapland almost by chance, when we researched the most northerly stops on the train line between Stockholm and Narvik. Abisko looked on the map like a tiny enclave surrounded by lakes and mountains. Reading more about it, we found that it was home to the Abisko blue hole – a unique microclimate where the geography creates frequent clear skies, making it one of the most reliable places on Earth to see the aurora borealis.

highlights.title: Asa Tribe barred from England Lions tour under Ebola rules after Kenya trip
highlights.summary: Glamorgan opener played for Jersey in Kenya last month. Entry ban brought in by St Kitts and Nevis government. The Glamorgan opener Asa Tribe has been barred from joining the England Lions tour of the Caribbean following a visit to Kenya and concerns over the recent outbreak of Ebola in east…
body: Tribe, 22, is able to represent his native Jersey until he wins a first senior England cap and played three List A games for the associate nation in Nairobi last month. From there he was due to join the England Lions squad in St Kitts and Nevis.

However, the emergence of the deadly Ebola virus in Kenya – with nine confirmed cases, including two fatalities – has seen the government of St Kitts and Nevis place an entry ban on recent non-national visitors to the country.

A spokesperson for the England and Wales Cricket Board said: “Asa Tribe was unable to enter Saint Kitts & Nevis, having recently travelled to Kenya. Saint Kitts & Nevis currently have a 21-day non-entry rule in place for non-nationals who have been in Kenya due to the Ebola situation in Kenya and seven other countries in Africa. Asa is back in the UK, and we are in touch with the relevant authorities.”

It is understood that after playing his final match in Nairobi on 27 October, Tribe was then intending to travel to St Kitts and Nevis using connecting flights. He had made it as far as Paris before discovering the problem.

Typing to a soundtrack of his own best reviews (“The world needs to hear your story”), an emboldened Will is soon exploring grislier avenues, including home invasion and murder, while his increasingly unhinged rants to creative-writing students attract a rapt protege. There is, he posits, only so much muscle one can wield while hunched over a laptop.

highlights.title: A new start after 60: At 26, I saw my dream Porsche. At 68, I built one from scratch
highlights.summary: Bill Drysdale could never afford the sports car he fell in love with as a young man. So when he retired, he went to night school to learn welding, and began assembling it, bit by bit... When he was 26, Bill Drysdale saw a Porsche 904 at Silverstone racetrack and fell in love.
body: Drysdale grew up in Wigtown, Scotland, and cars were in his blood – his grandfather was chauffeur to the local creamery manager, and he first saw a race with his father, when he was 12 – around the time that his mother went into hospital with multiple sclerosis. Drysdale, an only child, grew close to his father. At 14, he taught him to drive. Together they’d huddle in the kitchen to listen to the Le Mans 24 Hour race on the radio.
Drysdale was only 21 when his dad died; his mother ended up staying in hospital for 23 years. “That made me very independent,” he says. Determined? “Pig-headed, some would say.”

After studying maths and physics at the University of Glasgow, he joined a brake manufacturer as a graduate apprentice engineer. “Oh, it was tremendous,” he says. “As young chaps in the company, there was always this interest in cars and racing and competition.” His favoured form was “sprinting – racing against the clock, competing against yourself”. It was while playing mechanic to a friend in the pit at Silverstone that he saw the Porsche 904 and was floored by “the sound, the look, the line”.
